t: #2522 Partition String Into Substrings With Values at Most K
o: Greedily grow the current substring while its numeric value stays ≤ k; when appending the next digit would exceed k, start a new substring. Since digits are 1–9 (no zeros), every single digit is a valid piece as long as k ≥ 9... more precisely as long as k ≥ each digit; if any digit alone exceeds k, return −1. Example 1 (k=60): "165462" → "16","54","6","2" = 4 pieces. Example 2 (k=5): digit 8 > 5 → −1. Greedy is optimal because extending the current piece never hurts future choices (exchange argument).
k: Greedy: extend the current piece while cur·10 + d ≤ k, else cut.
If a single digit exceeds k, no good partition exists.
Values fit easily: cur ≤ k ≤ 10⁹, so cur·10 + d < 2⁶³ — no overflow concerns in practice (still fine in 64-bit).

a.i: Keep the running value of the current piece; cut whenever the next digit would overflow k, counting pieces.
s: For each digit d: if d > k return −1; if cur·10 + d ≤ k, cur = cur·10 + d; else ans++, cur = d.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over the string.

a.i: dp[i] = minimum pieces for prefix s[:i]; dp[i] = 1 + min over j < i with value(s[j..i)) ≤ k. Since any valid piece has at most 10 digits (k < 10¹⁰), only check the last 10 start positions — O(10n). Useful template if the objective were weighted.
s: For each i, for len = 1..10 (bounded by k's digits): if the substring value ≤ k and dp[i−len] finite, relax dp[i].
a.t: O(10·n) — each position checks at most ⌈log₁₀ k⌉ piece lengths.

w: Lead with the greedy — it's provably optimal and O(1) space; mention DP if asked for a generalizable technique. Pitfalls: forgetting the −1 case (single digit exceeding k), and noting digits are 1–9 so no leading-zero complications. Follow-up: maximize the number of pieces, or partition into pieces whose values multiply to ≤ k.
